Article Title: Your AI shopping assistant could empty your account, top banks warn; says AI agents may …
Article Text:
What the banks are worried about

What the banks want to see happen

Proposed safeguards

Major banks around the world including NatWest, Bank of America, ING, Capital One, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, and New Zealand’s ASB Bank have issued a joint warning that AI-powered shopping bots could expose consumers to scams, fraud, and data-privacy breaches, as reported by Reuters. The warning from the banks comes as tech giants like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta are increasingly promoting AI agents as shopping tools, whereas retailers race to influence chatbot recommendations. As per the Reuters report, British retailer John Lewis reported that searches originating from AI agents jumped to 2.5% this year, up from just 0.3% a year ago. "They are concerned that AI agents may buy the wrong thing or spend too much – or even worse, lose their money to scams and fraud. They are not sure whether they will be protected or who they will need to go to if things ⁠go wrong," said Bank of America.In a new report, the banking coalition acknowledged that customers are genuinely enthusiastic about the potential of AI-driven shopping and eager to adopt it. But the report was equally clear that adoption is outpacing both industry standards and consumer protections, leaving a meaningful trust gap between what AI agents promise and what safeguards currently exist.The report noted that consumers remain unsure whether AI will actually act in their best interests, worrying that AI agents could buy the wrong item, overspend, or — in the worst case — lose their money to scams and fraud altogether, with little clarity on whether they'd be protected or who to turn to if something goes wrong.Specific risks flagged in the report include AI agents requesting and directly entering customers' card details into websites without adequate oversight, as well as agents potentially steering shoppers toward payment methods that offer weaker fraud protections than more secure alternatives.The coalition plans to bring a set of proposals to policymakers, including mandatory disclosure whenever an AI agent is involved in a transaction, greater transparency into how these agents actually make purchasing decisions, and stronger safeguards around customer data protection.The report also argued that both consumers and merchants should retain the freedom to choose which AI-powered e-commerce services they use, and called for different AI shopping systems to be interoperable with one another — rather than locking users into a single ecosystem's tools.To mitigate risks, banks plan to discuss proposals with policymakers, including:* Mandatory disclosure when an AI agent is involved in a transaction.* Greater transparency on how AI agents make decisions.* Stronger safeguards to protect customer data.* Ensuring consumers and merchants can freely choose which AI-powered services to use.* Interoperability across different AI commerce systems.
Article Summary: Major banks around the world have issued a joint warning that AI-powered shopping bots could expose consumers to scams, fraud, and data-privacy breaches. The warning comes as tech giants like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta are increasingly promoting AI agents as shopping tools.

Article Title: Marc Benioff says because of Microsoft, Salesforce could not invest in OpenAI; Salesforce CEO says: I knew Sam Altman very well, I was like...
Article Text:
Microsoft kept Salesforce out of OpenAI

Microsoft's 27% OpenAI stake kept Salesforce off the cap table

Salesforce's $50 million Anthropic investment from 2023 is now worth around $5 billion

Anthropic's Claude now runs Salesforce's Slack and Agentforce

Benioff lost out on OpenAI but never cut ties with it

Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff wanted a stake in OpenAI long before most of the tech industry was chasing one. Sam Altman turned him down, and Microsoft was the reason. Speaking on Alex Heath's Sources podcast, in an episode published on Tuesday, Benioff said OpenAI's ties to Microsoft, a direct rival to Salesforce in enterprise software, kept the door shut.So Salesforce went to OpenAI's biggest rival instead. That fallback, Anthropic, is now valued at $965 billion and preparing for a public listing. Benioff believes the bet could earn Salesforce "not just billions but maybe tens of billions of dollars.""I knew Sam Altman very well," Benioff said on the Sources podcast. "I was like, 'Hey, I'd really like to be investing now in the company.'" According to Benioff, Altman replied that the Microsoft relationship meant Salesforce was not allowed to invest.On paper, the block made sense. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI, uses its models in products that compete with Salesforce's, and sells OpenAI access through Azure. The two companies have reworked their deal twice since October 2025. The latest revision, in April, made Microsoft's licence to OpenAI technology non-exclusive and allowed OpenAI to serve customers on other clouds.Benioff did not claim foresight. "We felt like, whoa, we can't go here, we're going to have to go everywhere else," he told Heath, adding that it was "not because we were so smart.""Everywhere else" meant a wide spread of AI startups, including Hugging Face.Salesforce first joined an Anthropic funding round in early 2023 with about $50 million and kept investing in later rounds. By June this year, that stake was reportedly worth around $5 billion, a figure calculated after Anthropic's $65 billion raise. Salesforce has never disclosed exactly how much of the Claude maker it owns.An Anthropic IPO would put a public price on that holding and eventually give Salesforce a way to sell shares. Anthropic has confidentially filed draft paperwork with regulators, with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs reportedly leading the offering. Altman, meanwhile, has said OpenAI will not go public in 2026."It's because we have been pushed so close with Anthropic," Benioff said on the podcast, explaining why he expects such large returns.The investment has become a working partnership. Claude is the default model across Slack and runs Slackbot, which Salesforce says has saved its employees 8.1 million hours of work on an annualised basis. In August, the two companies launched Claudeforce, which brings Salesforce data into Claude through a plugin with 37 prebuilt sales skills, from meeting prep to pipeline reviews. Claude also serves as a reasoning model inside Agentforce.Money moves the other way too. In May, Benioff said Salesforce would likely spend $300 million on Anthropic tokens this year, much of it on coding.The Anthropic tie-up has not made Salesforce a one-model company. Both Dario Amodei and Altman appeared at Dreamforce 2026 in San Francisco last week, and Salesforce is adding OpenAI capabilities to Missionforce, its AI agent platform for government customers.Benioff used the same stage to call the so-called SaaSpocalypse "crazy nonsense" and to forecast that Salesforce would cross $50 billion in annual revenue next year.Three years after Altman said no, Salesforce holds an early stake in one of the world's most valuable AI companies and still has OpenAI in the room. For a company that was shut out, it ended up with a seat at both tables.
Article Summary: Microsoft's 27% OpenAI stake kept Salesforce off the cap table. Salesforce's $50 million Anthropic investment from 2023 is now worth around $5 billion. An Anthropic IPO would put a public price on that holding and eventually give Salesforce a way to sell shares.

Article Title: OpenAI expands GPT-6 lineup with cheaper, faster Sol and Luna models
Article Text:
Cheaper models built on the same foundation

How the new models perform

Key features

Availability

OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has now introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. The company claims that Sol is designed as a high-performance model optimised for complex reasoning, large-scale research and enterprise applications. On the other hand, Luna, is a lighter and more adaptive model which is built for everyday use cases and offer faster responses and lower compute requirements. Both the new models are created with OpenAI’s latest alignment techniques, including safeguards around recursive self-improvement (RSI) and improved oversight mechanisms. OpenAI also stressed on the fact that the launch reflects its commitment to balancing innovation with safety, ensuring that frontier AI systems remain under human control while scaling their capabilities.Earlier this month, OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra, which it describes as the most intelligent and aligned model it has built to date. Sol and Luna extend that same generation of intelligence downward, trained using similar methods as Astra but optimized to advance the frontier on cost efficiency rather than raw capability. OpenAI says the two new models bring Astra's advances in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable tiers.The economics are the headline change here. Thanks to improvements in caching and inference, OpenAI is cutting API prices for both models by 50% compared to their GPT-5.6 promotional pricing. GPT-6 Sol now costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, down from $4 and $20 respectively. GPT-6 Luna is even cheaper, dropping to $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, down from $0.20 and $1.20. Astra remains OpenAI's top recommendation when uncompromising performance matters most.OpenAI is positioning Sol in particular as a serious contender against rival models at a fraction of the cost. On AutomationBench, a test of real-world business workflows, the company says GPT-6 Sol at its highest effort setting outperforms Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 at max effort while costing just 9% as much per task. On Agents' Last Exam, which evaluates complex, long-horizon professional workflows, Sol scored 56.4% at max effort — ahead of Opus 5's best score in the same evaluation, at 60% lower cost per task.Coding performance also saw a notable jump. On FrontierCode, which grades AI-generated code on whether it's actually ready to merge into real codebases, OpenAI says Sol improved substantially over its GPT-5.6 predecessor and now matches Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 at a much lower price. On a separate software-engineering benchmark, DeepSWE, Sol scored within roughly one percentage point of Fable 5's best result while costing about 80% less per task.Factuality — long a weak point for large language models — also improved meaningfully. Based on OpenAI's internal evaluation using real conversations where users had previously flagged mistakes, Sol now makes roughly half as many factual errors as its predecessor, approaching Astra-level reliability at a fraction of the cost.* Sol: Advanced reasoning, multi‑step task automation, and integration with scientific and enterprise workflows.* Luna: Lightweight deployment, optimized for consumer applications, and faster performance on smaller devices.* Shared Advances: Improved multilingual support, adaptive memory, and enhanced contextual understanding across domains.GPT-6 Sol and Luna are rolling out today in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, while Free and Go users can access Luna through the desktop app. Neither model is yet available in standard Chat. Developers can access both through the OpenAI API as gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna. OpenAI said the rollout within ChatGPT will happen gradually throughout the day to keep the service stable.
Article Summary: OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. GPT-6 Sol is designed for complex reasoning, large-scale research and enterprise applications. Luna, is a lighter and more adaptive model which is built for everyday use cases. Both the new models are created with OpenAI’s latest alignment techniques.

Article Title: Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 is faster, cheaper and matches Fable 5.1 on most work
Article Text:
Anthropic's new Claude Opus 5.5 is 40% cheaper than Opus 5

Claude Opus 5.5 pricing undercuts Opus 5 on every token

Opus 5.5 leads benchmarks in coding and knowledge work

Anthropic adds Fable-level safeguards for biology and cybersecurity

Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its new Claude 5.5 family, and the biggest change is cost. The company says the new AI model performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5. It also generates output more than 30% faster than its predecessor.This is Anthropic's first release since it called for pacing the AI frontier, so safety features sit right next to performance. Opus 5.5 was tested before launch by external evaluators, including METR and Frontier Design. Anthropic says it scored the best of any model on its automated behavioural audit, which runs nearly 2,000 simulated scenarios. The model is available now on the Claude Platform as claude-opus-5-5, and on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure.Input tokens cost $4 (about Rs 350) per million and output tokens $20 (about Rs 1,760), both 20% lower than Opus 5. Cache reads, which Anthropic says make up most of the bill in agentic and coding work, drop 60% to $0.20 (about Rs 18) per million. Opus 5.5 also uses fewer tokens per task, which is where the overall 40% saving comes from.Subscribers benefit too. Anthropic is raising five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans. Users also get a rate limit reset they can save and use whenever they choose.On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Opus 5.5 scored 66.4%, ahead of Fable 5.1 at 55.8% and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 57.9%. On GDPval-AA v2.1, which tests real-world work across 44 occupations, it posted 1846 Elo against 1708 for Opus 5.Anthropic also shared results from actual workloads. One early tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in under a day. In an internal test, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 both rewrote HAProxy, a widely used load balancer, from C into Rust. Opus 5.5 finished in 9.5 hours against 12 and cost 51% less.The company says the model writes more clearly as well. It puts key information first and avoids jargon, which responds to a common complaint about Opus 5.Opus 5.5 matches Claude Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, so it ships with safeguards similar to those on Fable 5.1. Developers can still find and fix bugs in their own code, but most cybersecurity tasks will be rerouted to Opus 4.8. Vetted labs, startups and pharmaceutical firms can apply to a new Life Sciences Verification Program. Verified security practitioners will get access through an expanded Cyber Verification Program in the coming weeks.Anthropic acknowledges some limits. It says Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated, which makes its real-world behaviour harder to predict. The company is pairing its alignment work with these safeguards for that reason.Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 are due in the coming weeks. For now, Anthropic's cheapest Opus in a generation is also the one it rates safest, even though its own tests may not catch everything.
Article Summary: Anthropic's new Claude Opus 5.5 is 40% cheaper than its predecessor. The company says the new AI model performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work. It also generates output more than 30% faster than its predecessors. The model is available now on the Claude Platform.

Article Title: Donald Trump wants to rename AI; says: 'artificial' makes AI sound fake, renames it 'super intelligence'; It is exactly the opposite of...
Article Text:
Trump picked 'super intelligence' after two social media polls

US president says whoever wins super intelligence wins the world

Superintelligence already has a very different meaning in AI research

US President Donald Trump wants the world to stop saying "artificial intelligence". Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday (September 22), Trump said the US will now officially call the technology "super intelligence", or SI. His reason is simple: the word "artificial" makes it sound fake. "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," he said.The change, according to Trump, will cover all US government documents. "From this point forward, all of the United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, super as opposed to artificial," he told the assembly. There is no word yet on when the switch will happen or how it will be carried out. Trump himself did not sound too sure. "Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't, we're gonna find out pretty soon," he said.The idea did not come out of nowhere. On Saturday (September 19), Trump posted on X and Truth Social that "many people think that the words 'Artificial Intelligence' are inaccurate, and very ineloquent." He then asked followers to vote on three options: Superior Intelligence, Extreme Intelligence and Supreme Intelligence."Superior Intelligence" took an early lead with around 39% of the vote and later crossed 41%. Then, on Monday, Trump ran a second poll that pitted "Superior Intelligence" against a new entry, "Super Intelligence". The new option won comfortably, and Trump started using "SI" in his posts almost immediately. So the name he announced at the UN was not even on the original ballot.The same weekend, Trump said he was forming an "AI Force", modelled on the Space Force from his first term. He also promised to name an AI czar soon, adding, "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" He did not explain what either would do.At the UN, the rename came wrapped in a larger message about the AI race. "Whoever wins super intelligence wins," Trump said, adding that the US is "leading now over China by a lot."He was clear that his government will not slow the technology down. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution," he said. He added that the Department of Justice and other law enforcement bodies would "watch it closely" and step in if needed. In the same breath, he argued that the fear around AI gets it wrong. "In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports," he said.Trump also lumped AI safety warnings with climate change and the "Russia, Russia, Russia hoax". Earlier in the week, he had called the backlash against AI a hoax pushed by his political rivals. The comments come after an Anthropic researcher resigned, saying leading AI companies believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade." Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has since proposed a plan to "pace the frontier", which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk appeared to back.There is a catch with Trump's pick. In AI circles, "superintelligence" is not a new word. Philosopher Nick Bostrom described it back in 1997 as "an intellect that is much smarter than the best human brains in practically every field." Researchers use it for hypothetical future systems that outperform humans across most tasks. Today's chatbots are not there yet, and Bostrom's work is largely about the risks such systems could pose."Artificial intelligence" itself has no legal status that a president can overwrite. Computer scientist John McCarthy coined it in a 1955 proposal for a Dartmouth College conference, co-authored with Claude Shannon, Marvin Minsky and Nathaniel Rochester. At the time, rival labels such as "automata studies" and "complex information processing" were also doing the rounds. "AI" won, and it has stuck for 70 years. It is even part of company names like OpenAI.Trump has renamed things before. The Gulf of Mexico and Denali got new labels, and digital maps in the US updated within days. A word used by millions of engineers, companies and users every day is a different test. Government files may say SI soon. Whether anyone outside Washington follows is the part Trump admitted he cannot predict.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump wants the world to stop saying "artificial intelligence" Trump said the US will now officially call the technology "super intelligence" or SI. The change, according to Trump, will cover all US government documents. There is no word yet on when the switch will happen or how it will be carried out.

Article Title: Apple is building a screenless Whoop rival, but it may not launch before 2028
Article Text:
Apple Watch is already copying Whoop and Oura, a band is the next step

Apple is developing a screenless fitness tracker to take on Whoop, the wearable maker now valued at around $10 billion. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple has spent several months exploring the category and is now building prototypes of a band that drops the display entirely.The early hardware pairs a thin fabric strap with a small computing module packed with sensors. Apple hasn't decided whether the product will ship. The project sits in an internal stage called a "technology investigation," and even if it moves ahead, a launch before 2028 looks unlikely. Apple declined to comment.The idea has backing from the top. Gurman reports that executive chairman Tim Cook and services chief Eddy Cue have taken a keen interest. Cue took over Apple's health teams late last year and has pushed them to borrow from newer rivals built around simpler interfaces. Engineers from Apple's Vision hardware group, the team behind Vision Pro, have also worked on the tracker.Markets noticed. Garmin, which sells display-free bands of its own, saw its shares fall as much as 2.5% after the report, while Apple stock rose about 1%.Apple remains one of the biggest smartwatch sellers, especially in the US.But Whoop and Oura have each built user bases in the millions by offering focused health tracking without apps or notifications. Oura filed for its IPO this month and is looking to raise up to $2.2 billion, while Whoop has said a listing is on the table. Google has entered the space too, with the Fitbit Air.Apple has already started borrowing from this crowd. The Apple Watch Series 12 and the revamped Health app bring a daily readiness score, more advanced heart rate tracking and an estimate of biological age. Whoop and Oura users will find all three familiar.The work also comes during a leadership change in Apple's health division. Former COO Jeff Williams retired at the end of last year, while Apple Watch marketing lead Stan Ng and fitness chief Jay Blahnik have both left.A screenless band would give Apple something it currently lacks: a way to sell its health tracking to people who don't want a smartwatch, including those unwilling to give up a mechanical watch. Before that, Apple is expected to launch smart glasses and camera-equipped AirPods in 2027, with a redesigned Apple Watch due as early as late 2027.
Article Summary: Apple is developing a screenless fitness tracker to take on Whoop and Oura. The company is building prototypes of a band that drops the display entirely. Early hardware pairs a thin fabric strap with a small computing module. The project sits in an internal stage called a "technology investigation"

Article Title: Xbox lays off 268 more employees across Halo Studios and other first-party studios; company says: This brings us roughly three-quarters of...
Article Text:
Xbox is now three-quarters of the way through its 3,200-job restructuring

Activision will build the next Halo game with a new team

Xbox is merging Forza studios and moving Obsidian under Bethesda

Ninja Theory faces closure after two failed sale deals

Microsoft is cutting another 268 jobs at Xbox, and the latest round lands hardest on the studio behind its most famous franchise. Halo Studios, formerly 343 Industries, is losing staff alongside other first-party teams and the Xbox Game Studios management and central functions layer. In the same move, the next mainline Halo game is being handed to Activision, the Call of Duty publisher.Xbox chief content officer Matt Booty announced the cuts in a memo to employees. They count towards the 3,200 role reductions that Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced in July for Microsoft's 2027 financial year, which ends in June 2027. About 1,600 of those jobs went in the first round. "The actions completed since July, inclusive of the studio divestitures, bring us roughly three-quarters of the way through previously announced restructuring," Booty wrote.Activision is setting up a purpose-built Halo team, kept separate from its Call of Duty development. A small group at Halo Studios will stay on to support the community and the games already in players' hands. The shift comes just months after Halo: Campaign Evolved launched.Activision is also taking charge of World's Edge, the Age of Empires studio, and Rare, the developer of Sea of Thieves. Activision president Rob Kostich said the aim is to "make the greatest Halo game ever."Booty says the goal is to run fewer business units and bring together groups that already work closely. Bethesda now oversees Obsidian, which continues work on Grounded and a new Fallout project made with Bethesda Game Studios. King, the Candy Crush maker, absorbs Microsoft Casual Games, home to Solitaire and Minesweeper.Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios, partners on Forza for over a decade, will now operate as one studio handling both Forza and Fable.The plan to offload studios has had mixed results. Compulsion Games and Double Fine went independent in August with their IP, back catalogues and runway funding. Undead Labs has now followed on similar terms and, with a new publisher, will still release State of Decay 3 on Game Pass on day one.Ninja Theory, the Hellblade developer, was not as lucky. Two separate agreements to sell the studio fell through, so Xbox will begin consultation with employees on a proposed closure while exploring other paths. Talks over Arkane's future in France are expected to run until the end of the year.The reason behind all of this was laid out in Sharma's July memo. Xbox was operating at margins three to 10 times lower than comparable platform and publishing businesses, and in a typical year lost 64 cents for every dollar it invested in studios. Employees will gather at an October 6 town hall, where Booty plans to look ahead to what he calls one of the strongest game lineups in Xbox history. With a quarter of the cuts still to come, that lineup now carries the weight of the reset.
Article Summary: Halo Studios, formerly 343 Industries, is losing staff. Activision is setting up a purpose-built Halo team, kept separate from its Call of Duty development. Activision president Rob Kostich said the aim is to "make the greatest Halo game ever"

Article Title: Nuuk launches SĒRV MAX multi-cook Kettle with EvenHeat technology
Article Text:
Nuuk launches SĒRV MAX multi-cook Kettle price and availability

Nuuk has launched SĒRV MAX, claiming it to be India’s first 100% food-safe multi-cook kettle featuring its EvenHeat engineered coil. Designed and made in India, SĒRV MAX has a 700W EvenHeat G-Type Coil, which wraps around the entire base of the kettle covering 35% more surface area than a conventional C-type element to distribute heat more evenly. It is paired with SĒRV WARM Mode which maintains cooked food at a steady 65°C until it is ready to be served. The appliance features 1.3L capacity, 2+1 cooking modes, and a SteelTech SUS304 stainless-steel interior, while the SteamTray included in the launch bundle adds another layer of functionality to it.The Nuuk SĒRV MAX is available at a launch price of Rs 2,699, with the SteamTray included, in Nuuk Red and Serene Grey colours. It is available on Nuuk website (Amazon, Blinkit and offline availability to go live by October).The product is made in India through Nuuk’s India-based manufacturing partnerships, reflecting the brand’s approach to building appliances around the realities of Indian homes. From chai and Maggi to idlis, dal and quick meals between busy schedules, it has been developed with food habits and everyday kitchen routines in mind.With its extra-large capacity, SĒRV MAX is built to accommodate approximately five cups at a time, offering more room for everyday preparations beyond a single cup of tea or coffee. Its two heat levels, alongside SĒRV WARM, allow it to adapt across different cooking needs, from boiled eggs and breakfast preparations to noodles, soup and rice.The SteamTray, with a 200 cm² steaming area, adds another layer of versatility, allowing users to steam momos, dumplings and vegetables.The product features SteelTech, a SUS304 stainless-steel interior that is food-grade, rust-proof and designed for everyday cooking without a conventional non-stick coating. This provides a durable cooking surface without relying on coatings that can scratch or flake with use.The appliance also features 5-Layer Ultimate SafetyTech, combining auto cut-off, boil-dry protection, overheat protection and thermal fuse protection. Its SafeTouch cool-touch body is designed to remain comfortable to hold even while the contents are boiling inside.“We believe that familiar appliances deserve to evolve with the way we live today. The kettle has long been a convenient part of Indian kitchens, but there is an opportunity to make it far more useful without making it more complicated. With SĒRV MAX, we set out to rethink this everyday format through more consistent heating, the flexibility to cook and keep food warm, a larger capacity, and a food-safe stainless-steel interior, rust-free, leach-free and heat-stable for daily boing and cooking. The kettle has been designed with real Indian cooking routines in mind, from the EvenHeat technology to the SĒRV WARM Mode. Our goal is to make everyday cooking more convenient,considered and safe, while staying true to our belief that thoughtful design should always serve a real consumer need,” said Gazal Kalra, Co-Founder, Nuuk.
Article Summary: SĒRV MAX has a 700W EvenHeat G-Type Coil, which wraps around the entire base of the kettle covering 35% more surface area than a conventional C-type element. The appliance features 1.3L capacity, 2+1 cooking modes, and a SteelTech SUS304 stainless-steel interior, while the SteamTray included in the launch bundle adds another layer of functionality.

Article Title: Palo Alto Networks taps Anthropic and OpenAI to automate corporate cyber defence
Article Text:
Always-on offensive testing and attack path mapping

Palo Alto Networks has announced an enterprise-grade cybersecurity service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) models from Anthropic and OpenAI , aiming to identify and neutralise network vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them. The deployment comes as cybercriminals increasingly rely on automated algorithms to locate and breach enterprise weaknesses, prompting security companies to build counter-defenses capable of matching automated hacking cycles. Dubbed Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, the platform pairs open-weight architectures with cybersecurity-tailored systems, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Cyber.Unlike traditional periodic vulnerability scans, the service operates as an always-on offensive testing engine built to adapt alongside evolving enterprise environments. According to the company, the system continuously evaluates web applications, application programming interfaces (APIs), and cloud infrastructure. It maps out complete end-to-end attack paths, allowing corporate defenders to pinpoint exposed entry points and hidden exploit vectors.“Threat actors today are deploying AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities, compressing breach cycles by almost 97% in some cases, from weeks to hours. To help defenders answer the critical question of whether they are prepared for this step-change in cybersecurity, Unit 42 is now offering continuous offensive testing to identify and validate vulnerabilities, pinpoint exposures and attack paths, and then accelerate remediation,” the company said.Beyond locating security gaps, Palo Alto Networks stated that the service delivers actionable mitigation guidance. This includes step-by-step code repairs alongside virtual patching solutions to shield assets before a permanent fix is integrated.“Palo Alto Networks developed and validated this approach over six months of in-house testing and across more than 100 Unit 42 customer engagements, backed by a $17 million investment in R&D and methodology optimization. During internal deployment within Palo Alto Networks, the company found a year's worth of exposures in three weeks. In customer assessments, the Frontier AI Exposure Analysis found exposures in 100% of customers. Of those, 37% rated high or critical in severity. Overall, most exposures stemmed from first-party apps and more than two in three exposures in third-party apps had no known CVE,” the company added.The company confirmed that the tool will be available internationally on an annual subscription basis. Pricing tiers will depend directly on the specific combination of OpenAI, Anthropic, and open-source models chosen by each enterprise client.
Article Summary: Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense is an always-on offensive testing engine built to adapt alongside evolving enterprise environments. It maps out complete end-to-end attack paths, allowing corporate defenders to pinpoint exposed entry points and hidden exploit vectors. Palo Alto Networks found a year's worth of exposures in three weeks.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos bought two neighbouring Indian Creek estates for $68 million and $79 million; his Florida property spending reached $237 million
Article Text:
PC: Forbes

Bezos’ first Indian Creek deal covered 2.8 acres and 9,300 square feet

The second Indian Creek estate brought Bezos’ total to $147 million

Two adjoining estates created 4.6 acres of waterfront land

A third purchase lifted Bezos’ Florida spending to $237 million

Indian Creek is a small community with very limited housing

Bezos’ latest Florida acquisitions bring his property spending to $237 million

Jeff Bezos has been steadily expanding his footprint in one of Florida’s most closely guarded residential enclaves. The Amazon founder first bought a waterfront home on Indian Creek Island for $68 million, then followed it with a neighbouring estate that cost another $79 million. Together, the two properties gave him a continuous 4.6-acre stretch of waterfront land in the small community near Miami.The purchases were already enough to make Indian Creek a significant part of Bezos’ property holdings. According to Forbes Global Properties, a third Florida acquisition has since pushed the amount he has spent on property in the state to about $237 million, adding another substantial purchase to a real estate portfolio that already spans several parts of the United States.Bezos’ first move on Indian Creek came earlier in the year, when he paid $68 million for 11 Indian Creek Island Road. The three-bedroom residence covers nearly 9,300 square feet and occupies a waterfront site measuring about 2.8 acres.The purchase gave Bezos a sizeable presence on the island before he added the property next door. Rather than being separate holdings scattered around the community, the two homes sit beside one another, creating a much larger continuous parcel of waterfront property.That second acquisition changed the scale of the purchase considerably.The neighbouring estate at 12 Indian Creek Island Road was sold to Bezos for $79 million, according to the Multiple Listing Service as mentioned by Forbes. The transaction brought the combined price of his two Indian Creek purchases to $147 million.Built in 2000, the seven-bedroom property occupies roughly 1.8 acres on the western side of Indian Creek. Its position gives the house views towards Biscayne Bay as well as the golf course belonging to the Indian Creek Country Club.As reported by Forbes Global Properties, the residence is considerably larger than the first home, with about 19,000 square feet of interior living space. It also has 200 feet of water frontage, 14 bathrooms and a six-car garage.Inside, the house follows a more traditional European-inspired style. Marble floors, tall ceilings and elaborate finishes run through the main living areas, while several rooms are designed specifically for entertaining and leisure.There is a wine cellar, a hosting salon and a room centred around a fireplace. A private cinema is also part of the property, while outside there is a heated swimming pool and a separate cabana house.The significance of the two purchases lies partly in their proximity. Bezos now controls the adjoining properties rather than simply owning two unrelated homes elsewhere on the island. The first property accounts for about 2.8 acres, while the second sits on another 1.8-acre lot. Combined, that amounts to roughly 4.6 acres of contiguous waterfront land.The arrangement also gives the Amazon founder access to two substantial residences, rather than requiring one house to accommodate all of the functions associated with a large estate. The larger mansion alone has seven bedrooms and 14 bathrooms, while the neighbouring property adds another home to the holding. For a community where land is limited by the size of the island itself, putting neighbouring parcels together represents a sizeable expansion of any individual owner's footprint.The Indian Creek deals were not the end of Bezos’ property spending in Florida. A third purchase brought his total expenditure on Florida real estate to about $237 million. That figure puts the two Indian Creek acquisitions into a wider pattern of major property purchases rather than treating them as an isolated investment. The $68 million and $79 million transactions account for $147 million of the reported total, leaving about $90 million attributable to the third acquisition.The exact scale of the latest purchase also illustrates how quickly Bezos’ Florida holdings have grown. Within the same period, his property interests moved from a single Indian Creek residence to neighbouring estates and then to a broader Florida portfolio worth hundreds of millions of dollars.Indian Creek Village sits on a man-made barrier island just outside Miami. Despite its proximity to one of the country's major cities, it is a remarkably small residential community, with fewer than 50 homes spread across an island of about 300 acres.The community is often referred to as the “Billionaire Bunker”, largely because of the wealth of some of its residents and the level of security surrounding the island. Privacy is a significant feature of the setting, with controlled access helping separate the residential enclave from the much busier Miami area nearby.Indian Creek Country Club occupies much of the island, while the residential properties sit along its waterfront edges. That limited supply of homes has made large parcels particularly unusual. Bezos’ two adjoining estates therefore give him a substantial presence within a community where there are relatively few residential properties to begin with.The Indian Creek acquisitions also fit into Bezos’ long-running interest in high-value residential real estate. His holdings have included properties in places such as New York, Washington, DC and Maui. One of his better-known purchases came in 2020, when he paid $165 million for a Beverly Hills estate. That transaction alone ranked among the most expensive residential property deals in the United States at the time.His property spending has continued across several locations since then. The Florida purchases add another major cluster to that portfolio, with the latest reported total of $237 million covering three acquisitions in the state.For Indian Creek, however, the most visible change is concentrated in a small section of the island. Bezos now owns two neighbouring waterfront estates, with the combined 4.6 acres giving him a much larger continuous property holding than either purchase would have provided on its own.
Article Summary: Bezos first bought a waterfront home on Indian Creek Island for $68 million, then followed it with a neighbouring estate that cost another $79 million. The two properties gave him a continuous 4.6-acre stretch of waterfront land in the small community near Miami. A third purchase brought his total expenditure on Florida real estate to about $237 million.
